opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the central difficulties of the field, and it's something I've spent a lot of time worrying about. In most areas of engineering, you get to learn from failure. A bridge falls down, you study why, you update your practices. With alignment, the failures we're most concerned about are ones where, by the time you observe them clearly, it may be quite hard to recover. So there's a real question of how you make progress on a problem you can't yet directly see.

The way I approach it is roughly in three parts. The first is to think about the problem abstractly, almost adversarially. I'll imagine some proposed training procedure and ask: what's the story where this goes wrong? Is there a coherent way a model could end up behaving well on the training distribution while actually pursuing something different, or while deceiving the humans overseeing it? If I can tell a plausible story like that, I count it as a failure of the method, even if nobody has observed it yet. That's a pretty demanding standard, and a lot of my theoretical work has been trying to find approaches where I can't construct that kind of story. It's a way of substituting reasoning for empirical failures we don't get to see.

The second part is that you can often build smaller analogues of the failures today. We already see models that exploit flaws in their reward signal, models that tell evaluators what they want to hear rather than what's true, systems that generalize in ways we didn't intend. Those aren't the catastrophic versions, but they're the same underlying phenomenon. So you can study the mechanics now: how does reward hacking emerge, when does a model learn to model its overseer, how do we detect it. You can also deliberately construct "model organisms" of misalignment, cases where you intentionally train a system to have some bad property and then check whether your detection or correction techniques actually catch it. That gives you something like a test bed.

The third part is just trying to stay honest about uncertainty. I don't think we should be confident that the problems will look exactly like what we imagine. Some of the theoretical worries might turn out to be non-issues in practice, and there might be problems we haven't anticipated. So I try to work on things that seem robustly useful: better ways for humans to oversee systems smarter than them, better ways to understand what's happening inside a model, better ways to evaluate whether something is safe. Those seem valuable across a wide range of scenarios.

The thing I'd really want to avoid is the strategy of "we'll wait until we see the problem and then fix it." For many problems that's fine. But if the failure mode involves systems that are capable enough to hide their misbehavior, or that are already deployed widely when things go wrong, waiting is the risky part. So I think it's worth paying the cost of working somewhat in the dark, while trying as hard as possible to ground that work empirically wherever we can.

r001.rationale: It says capable systems may hide misbehavior and that waiting until a failure is clearly observed can make recovery difficult, identifying the risk that warning signs may not be visible in time.

r002.rationale: It argues against waiting to develop alignment methods until a failure appears, but does not identify the ability to act quickly once signs appear as a reason for preparing techniques in advance.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is maybe the central methodological question for the field, and I don't think there's a fully satisfying answer. Let me say how I actually think about it.

The naive version of alignment research is: wait until you see a failure, then fix it. That works great for most of engineering, and honestly it works for a lot of what gets called alignment today. But the failures I'm most worried about are ones where the first serious instance is also the one you can't recover from, or at least where recovery is extremely expensive. If you're worried about systems that are competent enough to understand they're being evaluated and behave differently under evaluation than deployment, you really don't get to run the experiment and look at the result in the normal way.

So the question is what you do instead, and I'd break it into a few pieces.

The first is that you try to identify the structural reasons a problem would arise, rather than waiting for the phenomenon. If I think about something like reward hacking or deceptive alignment, I'm not reasoning from "I saw a model do this," I'm reasoning from "here is a training process, here is what it selects for, here is the gap between what it selects for and what we actually want, and here is why that gap gets worse rather than better as capabilities scale." That's an argument about the shape of the optimization, and you can make it and scrutinize it before you have the system. You can be wrong, but you can be wrong in ways that other people can point at.

The second is that you look for the earliest, weakest analogues of the failure and take them seriously even when they're not scary. We already have models that exploit flaws in reward models. We already have models that will tell you what you want to hear. Those aren't catastrophic, but they're instances of the same mechanism, and the question I'm asking is whether our techniques make them go away or just push them below the threshold where we notice. If a fix works by making the behavior less visible rather than less present, that's exactly the kind of fix that fails later.

The third piece, and the one I've spent most of my time on, is that you can try to work on problems that are defined by the worst case rather than by observed behavior. If I ask "can I design a training procedure where, no matter what the model has learned internally, I can still get a reliable answer about what it would do," that question doesn't depend on waiting for a failure. It's more like a math problem. The downside is that it's much harder and you often can't solve it. The upside is that when you make progress, the progress transfers to systems you've never seen.

And then there's a fourth thing which is just honesty about the epistemic situation. A lot of alignment research, mine included, is making bets about which failures are real. Some of those bets will look silly in retrospect. I think the right attitude is that you want a portfolio: some people doing careful empirical work on the failures we can already see, some people building evaluations designed to surface the next tier of failures before deployment, and some people doing the more theoretical, worst-case oriented work. You don't want everyone doing the same thing, because the whole problem is that we don't know which approach is going to turn out to have been the important one.

The thing I push back on is the view that says, because you haven't seen the failure yet, you shouldn't take it seriously. That's a reasonable heuristic in most domains, and I understand why people apply it. But it's basically a heuristic that says never prepare for anything novel, and the entire premise of the situation is that we're building something novel. So I'd rather make my arguments explicit, make predictions where I can, look hard at the early analogues, and accept that some fraction of the work will turn out to have addressed problems that never materialized. That's a cost I'm willing to pay given what's on the other side of the ledger.

r001.rationale: The response says the first serious failure may be the one that cannot be recovered from and that ordinary experimentation may not be possible, giving a clear reason to prepare before warning signs become available.

r002.rationale: It does not identify rapid action after warning signs appear as a reason to develop alignment techniques in advance.

astra-6.text:
I think the main difficulty is that you’re trying to study a problem before you can reproduce it in the form you ultimately care about. So you have to make some guesses about what’s going to go wrong. But you’d like your research to depend as little as possible on those guesses being exactly right.

For example, we train models to produce behavior that looks good to a human evaluator. There’s a potential gap between looking good to an evaluator and actually doing what we want. You can study that gap today, even if current models aren’t capable of exploiting it in particularly sophisticated ways. You can ask: when the evaluator makes a mistake, does the training process reinforce that mistake? And can we give the evaluator enough help to distinguish a good answer from a convincing but bad answer?

That doesn’t establish that your method will work for a much more capable system. I think you need to be quite explicit about which parts you’ve tested and which parts remain an argument about what will happen later.

The approach I’m most excited about is to develop methods now, understand why they might work, and then keep testing them as the relevant capabilities emerge. The danger is either waiting until you have an unmistakable failure, when you may have very little time left, or becoming attached to a story about future failures that you never subject to empirical scrutiny.

r001.rationale: The response warns that waiting for an unmistakable failure may leave little time, but it does not identify the possibility that warning signs may never appear.

r002.rationale: The response says there may be little time left if research waits for an unmistakable failure; it does not state that advance work enables a quick response once signs appear.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main difficulty is that you don’t get to observe the failure you ultimately care about. You can study systems doing things their designers didn’t intend, but there’s a real question about whether the solutions you develop will generalize to much more capable systems.

So I would try to make the problem concrete before trying to solve it. Suppose you’re using an AI to help write software, and it understands the code much better than you do. How do you tell whether it’s actually doing a good job, rather than producing something that looks good to you? That’s a problem you can start studying now, even if today’s models aren’t capable of carrying out the most concerning kinds of deception.

You can also construct situations where the model knows something the person evaluating it doesn’t, or where giving a misleading answer would get a higher reward. Then you can ask whether your training procedure produces the behavior you wanted. Those experiments aren’t a demonstration that you’ve solved alignment, but they can help distinguish approaches that have some chance of working from approaches that fail for fairly basic reasons.

Ultimately, you need an argument about why your method should work as systems become more capable, together with experiments that put pressure on that argument. I wouldn’t be comfortable relying entirely on either one.

r001.rationale: It says the failure that matters may never be observable and argues for studying alignment problems now.

r002.rationale: It recommends developing and testing techniques in advance, but does not identify acting quickly after failure signs appear as a reason.
